p.title: Computational and Graph-Theoretic Analysis of Legislative Networks: New Zealand's Mental Health Act as a Case Study

ext.title: Computational and Graph-Theoretic Analysis of Legislative Networks: New Zealand's Mental Health Act as a Case Study
ext.venue: Information (MDPI), vol. 17, no. 2, article 161; received 18 Dec 2025, accepted 3 Feb 2026, published 5 Feb 2026. Metadata hint confirmed.
ext.document_type: Journal article, open access (CC BY licence stated on p.1)
ext.coverage: Full text read in chunks: all 21 pages (extracted text lines 1-1196), including abstract, introduction, Sections 2-6, Tables 1-6, Figures 1-4 (captions and axis labels), conclusions, data availability and all 36 references. All 116 annotation items in _annots/d3b90168ce7a.json were read (114 highlights, 2 margin notes). Topics not covered by the paper: lobbying, elections, persuasion/turnout, resource allocation, legislator-level behaviour, path-finding algorithms (Katz counts paths but no path search is described), and text measurement beyond LDA topic modelling of Act summaries and keywords. paul_markup covered text is given as a short topical locator rather than verbatim, to respect the copyright rule; the exact covered_text strings remain in the annotation JSON.
ext.research_question: No explicit research question is stated. Stated aim (Sec. 1, p.3-4): (1) build a focal legislative citation network around a seed Act via depth-limited, layer-by-layer expansion, avoiding dominance by global hubs; (2) add LLM-assisted semantic representation of Acts; (3) detect thematic communities and check their alignment with NZ parliamentary committee domains. Scope limited to Acts (historical, repealed, active); court cases excluded (Sec. 1, p.4).
ext.theory: Only implicit. Influence is treated as accumulating through layered statutory dependence and procedural cascade risk (a change to one Act may force reconsideration of dependent Acts), operationalised with Katz prestige centrality (Sec. 3, p.12-13). Argues against PageRank (static formulation sensitive to network growth, citing [35]) and harmonic centrality (shortest-path proximity assumed to mean legal relatedness) on p.13. Also argues that focal, seed-centred subgraphs reveal local influence that whole-corpus rankings hide (Sec. 2, p.4-5). No formal model of legal influence is estimated.
ext.data: Unit: Act (node); edges are directed legal references from citing Act to cited Act. Corpus: 17,709 NZ Acts in XML (active, repealed, historical) from the NZ Parliamentary Counsel Office / legislation.govt.nz (Sec. 2.1, p.6). Seed: Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992. Subgraph sizes (Table 2, p.9): layer 1 = 27 Acts (0.15%); layer 2 = 2,159 (12.2%); layer 3 = 6,021 (34.0%). Six relation types: AMD, AMD_S, PR, PR_S, R_S, CIT. Period: no date range stated for the corpus; repealed and historical Acts are included. Validation samples: 50 relations per type, 300 total (Sec. 2.3, p.7); full-document validation on 10 Acts (p.7). LLM method run 10 times and averaged. Code is said to be at github.com/maryamild/Thesis (accessed 14 Jan 2026); the NZLII reference is dated "31 June 2025", which is not a valid date.
ext.method: 1) Rule-based NER and relation extraction on XML Acts using regular expressions triggered by phrases such as "inserted by", "repealed by", "within the meaning of" (Sec. 2.2, p.6-7). An LLM prompt-based extractor was tried and dropped for run-to-run variability and cost. 2) Breadth-first, layer-by-layer expansion from the seed, merging duplicate nodes by title and legislative ID, expanding only newly found nodes, stopping at three layers (Sec. 2.4, p.8-9). 3) Katz prestige centrality by power iteration, x_i = alpha * sum_j A_ji x_j + beta, beta typically 1, alpha < 1/lambda_max; directed graph with all six relation types as edges; rankings reported, not raw scores (Sec. 3, p.12-13). 4) Louvain community detection on 2-layer and 3-layer graphs, modularity reported (Sec. 4.1, p.15). 5) Two LDA topic models per Act: rule-based LDA on full legislative text (TF-IDF, lemmatisation, stopword removal) and LLM-assisted LDA on an LLM summary (max 150 words) plus 10-15 keywords, temperature 0, one pass per Act (Sec. 2.5, p.9-12). Number of topics and priors chosen by coherence score. 6) Jaccard similarity between community LDA keywords and predefined committee keyword sets; each community assigned to its best-matching committee (Sec. 4.2, p.16). 7) Agglomerative clustering merges similar Louvain communities into 6 macro-communities (Table 6, p.17).
ext.identification: None stated. Descriptive, computational network analysis on a single seed Act. No causal identification, no inferential statistics and no significance tests are reported; "influence" is a centrality score, not an estimated effect.
ext.scope: Population: all New Zealand Acts in the official XML corpus (17,709, including historical and repealed Acts), with analysis restricted to a seeded subgraph around one Act. Institution: NZ legislation and its parliamentary committee structure. Era: not defined; corpus is cumulative and undated in the text. Excluded: court cases and judicial interpretation (p.4). Authors state the method is jurisdiction-agnostic, but only NZ data is analysed.

key_findings.finding: Layered subgraph growth: the seed's 1-, 2- and 3-layer neighbourhoods reach 27, 2,159 and 6,021 Acts; 3 layers covers 34% of the corpus.
Authors stop expansion at three layers because the focal Act drops out of the top-50 Katz ranking beyond layer 3.
key_findings.numbers: Mental Health Act not in top 50 by Katz at layer 3

key_findings.finding: Rule-based relation extraction outperforms the LLM-based method on both precision and recall.
key_findings.numbers: Rule-based precision 0.96, recall 0.89. LLM average precision 0.86, recall 0.78. Text gives rule-based overall precision as 93% on 300 sampled relations (p.7), which does not match Table 1.

key_findings.finding: Mental Health Act is 2nd by Katz prestige in the 2-layer subgraph but falls out of the top 50 in the 3-layer subgraph. Authors read this as local, not systemic, centrality.

Other top-10 Katz movements: Legislation Act 2019 stays 1st; Secondary Legislation Act 2021 3rd to 2nd; Public Service Act 2020 9th to 7th; Criminal Procedure Act 2011 4th to 3rd; Corrections Act 2004 7th to 35th; Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003 8th to 37th; Policing Act 2008 10th to 14th.
Authors attribute the seed's high 2-layer rank partly to construction bias: the seed is the root, so many short paths pass through it. The bias fades as the network grows.
Louvain finds 14 communities (modularity 0.393) in the 2-layer graph and 15 communities (modularity 0.392) in the 3-layer graph.

Louvain communities align only weakly with committee keyword sets (Jaccard). Several committees repeat across communities; the authors then merge communities into 6 macro-communities, which raises the Maori Affairs match to the top score.
key_findings.numbers: Best Jaccard scores: 0.66 (community 1, Maori Affairs), 0.50 (several), range 0.10-0.67; macro-community Maori Affairs 0.67, Foreign Affairs 0.50, Transport 0.36, Education 0.29, Justice 0.23, Finance 0.14

key_findings.finding: LLM-assisted LDA gives a more concentrated, procedure-free topic set for the seed Act than rule-based LDA, which mixes in procedural words such as section and subsection.
key_findings.numbers: Top topic weight 0.43 (LLM) vs 0.37 (rule-based); second 0.28 vs 0.33; third 0.19 vs 0.21

key_findings.finding: Authors claim LLM-assisted LDA gives higher-coherence topics; no coherence values are reported anywhere in the paper.

limitations: Construction bias: the seed Act is the root of its own subgraph, so its centrality is partly structural (authors' own admission, Sec. 3, p.13). Results at 2 layers are most affected.
The 3-layer cap is a judgement trade-off (thematic relevance vs processability), not an optimised or tested choice (Sec. 2.4, p.8).

Internal inconsistency: text reports 93% rule-based precision (p.7); Table 1 reports 0.96 (p.8). Sampling basis for recall (10-Act full-document validation vs 300-relation sample) is not fully specified.
Validation is a manual check by the authors; no inter-coder reliability or independent gold standard is reported.
LLM stochasticity is acknowledged (Sec. 2.2, 2.3) but Sec. 2.5.2 says temperature 0 and single pass give consistent outputs; no run-to-run variance numbers are reported.
Coherence claims (higher coherence, cleaner separation) rest on qualitative reading of one Act's topics; no coherence scores or hyperparameter values are given.

Katz attenuation factor alpha and the exact beta are not reported, so the Katz results are not fully reproducible from the paper alone. Louvain resolution, random seed and agglomerative-clustering linkage and cut level are also unstated.
Only one seed Act and one jurisdiction are analysed; generalisability claims (Sec. 5-6) are asserted, not tested. No cross-jurisdiction or temporal results.
No time dimension: legal evolution and policy impact are named as aims but no temporal analysis is done; the paper defers this to future work.
Centrality choice is argued against PageRank and harmonic centrality, but no numerical comparison with those measures is shown.
Table 6 caption reads 'Columns 4-6' and its rows are a reduced set of the earlier table, so the mapping from communities to macro-communities is hard to follow.
Citation error: NZLII reference is dated 31 June 2025 (invalid date). Author acknowledgment discloses AI-assisted language editing.
The rule-based pipeline depends on hand-written regular expressions tuned to NZ drafting conventions; the authors say this is adaptable but do not show it on another corpus.
measures: Relation extraction precision and recall (TP/FP/FN against manual gold standard), Sec. 2.3
Katz prestige centrality rank (power iteration, directed graph, six relation types as edges), Sec. 3
Louvain modularity Q (0.393 two-layer; 0.392 three-layer), Sec. 4.1
Jaccard similarity between community keywords and committee keyword sets, Sec. 4.2
LDA topic weights per Act (top three topics for the seed Act), Table 3
Subgraph size and corpus coverage (count and % of 17,709), Table 2
Topic coherence used for hyperparameter selection (no values reported)
references_of_note: [2] Sakhaee, N. (2020). Structure and Evolution of Legislation Networks. PhD thesis, University of Auckland. Source of rule-based LDA on legal text and of the Katz-centrality justification used here; the authors' own prior work.
[35] Mariani, Medo & Zhang (2015). Ranking nodes in growing networks: When PageRank fails. Scientific Reports 5:16181. Cited against PageRank for legislative networks.
[36] Rochat, Y. (2009). Closeness centrality extended to unconnected graphs: the harmonic centrality index. Cited against harmonic centrality.

[22] Coupette, Beckedorf, Hartung, Bommarito & Katz (2021). Measuring law over time: a network analytical framework with an application to statutes and regulations in the US and Germany. Frontiers in Physics 9:658463. Closest prior work on legal-network measurement over time.
[25] Fortunato, S. (2010). Community detection in graphs. Physics Reports 486:75-174. Background for Louvain communities.
[23] Niu, Zeng, Fan & Di (2015). Robustness of centrality measures against network manipulation. Physica A. Relevant to centrality robustness, not tested here.
[28] Lee, Lee & Yang (2019). Network structure reveals patterns of legal complexity: the Constitutional legal network. PLoS ONE 14:e0209844. Legal-network precedent.
[6] Sulis et al. (2020). Exploring network analysis in a corpus-based approach to legal texts. COUrT workshop. Combines network and text analysis of legal corpora.
[15] Colombo, A. (2024). Leveraging knowledge graphs and LLMs to support and monitor legislative systems. CIKM 2024. Closest LLM-plus-legislative-graph work.
[16] Mohammadi et al. (2025). Combining topic modelling and citation network analysis of ECtHR case law. Artificial Intelligence and Law. Method precedent: topics plus citation network.
[17] Koniaris, Anagnostopoulos & Vassiliou (2018). Network analysis in the legal domain: EU legal sources. Journal of Complex Networks 6:243-268.
[19] Chiticariu, Li & Reiss (2013). Rule-based information extraction is dead! Long live rule-based IE systems! EMNLP 2013. Supports the rule-based extraction choice.
[29] Litaina et al. (2024). Towards LLM-based semantic analysis of historical legal documents. SemDH 2024. LLM extraction on legal text.
[5] Borner, Sanyal & Vespignani (2007). Network science. Annual Review of Information Science and Technology 41:537-607. General reference.
[10] NZ Parliamentary Counsel Office (2024). New Zealand Legislation (XML). Data source.

rel.summary_md:
Ardekani et al. build a citation network of New Zealand Acts. It is seeded on the Mental Health Act 1992 and grows breadth-first for three layers: 27, then 2,159, then 6,021 of 17,709 Acts. Edges are amendment, repeal and citation relations pulled from XML with hand-written regex rules. The rules beat an LLM extractor: precision 0.96 and recall 0.89 in Table 1, against 0.86 and 0.78 averaged over 10 LLM runs. The text gives 93% precision for the rules, which does not match the table.

Nodes are ranked by Katz prestige, which counts incoming paths. The seed Act ranks 2nd in the 2-layer graph and drops out of the top 50 at 3 layers. The authors call it "locally central but not systemically dominant" and say part of the 2-layer rank comes from the seed being the root of its own graph. Louvain finds 14 communities at modularity 0.393 and 15 at 0.392. These communities match committee keyword sets only weakly (Jaccard 0.10-0.67). There are no significance tests, no time dimension, and alpha, the Louvain resolution and the Louvain seed are not reported.

For Paul's systems the paper adds no causal evidence, but it sharpens two methodological points. First, centrality computed on a graph cut to one topic depends on where the cut is made. That bears on the Katz-Bonacich benchmark, which runs on the CU-only kernel, and on comparisons between sector networks. Second, a Louvain partition should come with its modularity and an external alignment check. Press HCoI reports neither. All nodes in the paper are statutes, not legislators. That limits every transfer to Melange's member graphs to the method, not the findings.

bearings.paper_claim: Katz prestige x_i = alpha*sum_j A_ji x_j + beta counts INCOMING directed paths. On one seed, rank depends strongly on graph radius: the Mental Health Act is 2nd at 2 layers (2,159 Acts) and outside the top 50 at 3 layers (6,021 Acts). Corrections Act goes 7th to 35th; HPCA Act goes 8th to 37th. Alpha is not reported.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 3, p.12-14; Table 4 p.13; Table 2 p.9
bearings.system_side: The KB benchmark sums OUT-walks on the live build_P kernel (b = sum_k (delta*A)^k 1, delta = 0.85/lambda_max). It runs on load_network(), which defaults to NET_CONFIG='cu', a CU-bill-bounded graph. It then Spearman-correlates the result with allocations, money and legislative score. It is diagnostic only, and the chain does not consume it.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the radius-sensitivity lesson transfers: rankings computed on a bounded subgraph are local. The paper's graph is a directed Act-citation DAG-like network, not a legislator kernel, and its Katz is prestige (in-direction), whereas Battaglini-Patacchini KB is out-direction. Paul's highlight of the paper's Katz choice therefore does not validate this benchmark's direction. A useful check would be to recompute KB on 'holistic' vs 'cu' and report rank stability, labelled UNVERIFIED until reproduced (DE-062). KB values are heuristic model outputs, never influence or access probabilities (D-025).

bearings.paper_claim: LDA topic representation plus Louvain gives 14 communities (Q=0.393, 2-layer) and 15 (Q=0.392, 3-layer), with modularity above 0.3 treated as meaningful. Alignment with external committee keyword domains is weak (best Jaccard 0.10-0.67; several committees repeat), and agglomerative merging into 6 macro-communities is needed to raise the matches.
bearings.system_side: Press HCoI builds topic profiles, links members at Pearson >= 0.6, runs Louvain (seed 7) and keeps communities of size >= 3. It reports no modularity and no external alignment score. Homophily replication at press resolution was null.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The pipeline (topic model -> similarity -> Louvain -> label check) is close enough that reporting modularity Q and an external alignment check (e.g., Jaccard against committee rosters or cosponsor communities) is a cheap, directly transferable addition. The paper's own Q and Jaccard values come from Act citation graphs and are not benchmarks for member press-profile graphs. Its weak committee alignment is a caution that topical communities need not match institutional structure.

bearings.paper_claim: Where the network boundary is drawn changes who is central: the top-10 Katz ranks reshuffle between the 2-layer and 3-layer subgraphs. The authors attribute part of the seed's 2-layer prominence to construction bias, because the seed is the root.
bearings.system_side: The NETWORKS registry defines separately bounded universes: cu (published), holistic, holistic_norm, bank_reg (CRS subject terms) and crypto (title screen). The system compares hub concentration and dyad novelty across them (bank_reg 76.1% novel vs CU; hub flag at 3x the second-highest degree).
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies in the abstract: cross-sector centralization comparisons depend on how each bill universe was screened, and a title screen (crypto) is not the same as subject terms (bank_reg). The paper bounds by citation hops from one seed, not by topic screen, so the size of the effect does not transfer. Any cross-config comparison should name its window and denominator.

bearings.paper_claim: The authors argue against PageRank for legislative networks because its static formulation is sensitive to network growth (citing Mariani, Medo & Zhang 2015). They show no numerical comparison with PageRank.
bearings.system_side: Staffer PageRank uses d = 0.85 as primary, with sensitivity runs at 0.70 and 0.95, on a layer-balanced walk with group-balanced teleport. It is descriptive, with no composite influence score.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak. The growth or age-bias critique applies to citation networks, where old nodes accumulate in-links. The staffer graph is a co-tenure graph, so the argument transfers only if snapshots are compared across vintages. The paper offers no evidence, only an argument.

gaps_exposed: Press HCoI Louvain output reports no modularity Q and no external alignment check (committee or cosponsor-community overlap). The paper reports both.

No radius or boundary sensitivity test for centrality: the KB benchmark and the cosponsor InfluenceScore are computed on the CU-bounded graph only, and nobody has measured how ranks move on the holistic universe.
Regex topic tagging (CATEGORIES in cu_press_release_scraper.R:1739) has no per-category precision/recall sample. The paper's 50-items-per-type validation gives a template.
The underdog lens still uses Centrality% from a topic-bounded cosponsor graph. The paper's local-versus-systemic finding suggests labelling that input as local to the CU universe.
flags: Paul's 'Important! Coalition' margin note on Louvain: the paper's communities are clusters of STATUTES in a citation graph, not legislator coalitions, and they align only weakly with committee domains (Jaccard 0.10-0.67). Any carryover to member coalitions is analogical. Melange already uses Louvain (press HCoI; the positive-Louvain seed in signed coalitions), and HCoI homophily came back null.

Wording: the paper calls Katz rank 'influence' that 'propagates'. Under D-025, graph ranks are heuristic model outputs, never influence, closeness or access probabilities, so do not import that language.
Acronym collision: 'LDA' in this paper means Latent Dirichlet Allocation, not the Lobbying Disclosure Act. This is unrelated to D-021 (LDA filings as an identity source only).

Direction mismatch: Paul highlighted the paper's Katz PRESTIGE, which counts in-paths, while the system's Katz-Bonacich benchmark counts out-walks (kb_benchmark.py:33-40). The highlight does not validate the benchmark.

The paper is internally inconsistent: rule-based precision is 93% in the text (p.7) and 0.96 in Table 1 (p.8). Alpha, the Louvain resolution and seed, and the clustering linkage are unreported, so the results cannot be reproduced from the paper.
The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). No conflict there.
Any reanalysis suggested here (e.g., KB rank stability across NET_CONFIGs) stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
rel.paul_alignment:
Paul's takeaways are mostly accurate. Two parts are stale relative to the system as built.

(1) His note that NER/IE could feed data extraction is right, but the paper actually rejected LLM extraction in favour of deterministic regex on XML (precision 0.96 vs 0.86). That matches how Melange's collectors already work: regex category tagging and BILLSTATUS XML. His margin question 'Same for the US?' has a yes answer the system already uses: BILLSTATUS XML and the uscode.house.gov sentinel.

(2) 'Louvain can find communities and coalitions' predates the system's own use. Louvain already runs in press HCoI (seed 7), where homophily was null, and seeds the signed-coalition search. The paper also shows weak alignment between Louvain communities and committee domains, which undercuts a direct coalition reading.

(3) His 'more research on centrality is needed' is consistent with the system. It retired direction-blind cosponsor centrality (AB13 = 0), keeps Katz-Bonacich as a diagnostic only, and runs damping sensitivity on staffer PageRank. The paper's sharpest contribution is that centrality on a bounded subgraph is local, and his notes do not record it.

His stated drawback (citations only; no lobbying, co-sponsorship or money) is correct.

related.why: Both use a topic model (LDA) and then Louvain to find communities. Malaterre is the direct template for fec/network/press_hcoi.py, and Paul cross-references the two.
Battaglini & Patacchini's out-direction Katz-Bonacich is what kb_benchmark.py implements. Ardekani's in-direction Katz prestige is a different quantity, so the two should not be conflated.
Ardekani checks thematic communities against committee domains. Porter supplies the committee-network structure of the US House, which would be the external reference for an equivalent US check.

Both are network-centrality studies of legislation. Sotoudeh works on member cosponsorship and bill passage, Ardekani on statute citation. Together they show that centrality conclusions depend on graph construction.
Kim & Kunisky detect communities in lobbying networks, which is the actor-level coalition setting Paul says Ardekani's citation-only framework does not cover.
Aref & Neal partition signed legislator networks into coalitions. That is the coalition reading Paul's margin note wants from Louvain, which Ardekani's unsigned Act graph cannot provide.

paul_entries.text:
Ardekani, Iman, et al. “Computational and Graph-Theoretic Analysis of Legislative Networks: New Zealand’s Mental Health Act as a Case Study.” MDPI, Multidisciplinary Digital Publishing Institute, 5 Feb. 2026, www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/17/2/161.

The article presents a case study of a computational framework used to analyze legislative citations for a single act in the New Zealand Parliament. This framework can be applied to the present research regarding how they mathematically compute the various nodes, vertices, and vectors. Additionally, machine learning methods used in the article, such as Named Entity Recognition (NER) or IE, can be applied to data extraction and processing in the applied product. Finally, the combination of structural graph analytics and semantic representation offers a potential layer to the ultimate analysis. The main drawback of this article is that it focuses on the legal citations of a bill and does not track key elements of lobbying and consulting, such as co-sponsorships, monetary congestion, or other variables. More thought will be needed as to how this can be practically applied to the intended product. However, the article goes into depth on the Louvian method, which can be used by communities and coalitions. Additional research into different forms of centrality is needed.

Ardekani, Iman, et al. “Computational and Graph-Theoretic Analysis of Legislative Networks: New Zealand’s Mental Health Act as a Case Study.” *MDPI*, Multidisciplinary Digital Publishing Institute, 5 Feb. 2026, [www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/17/2/161](http://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/17/2/161).

The article presents a case study of a computational framework used to analyze legislative citations for a single act in the New Zealand Parliament. This framework can be applied to the present research regarding how they mathematically compute the various nodes, vertices, and vectors. Additionally, machine learning methods used in the article, such as Named Entity Recognition (NER) or IE, can be applied to data extraction and processing in the applied product. Finally, the combination of structural graph analytics and semantic representation offers a potential layer to the ultimate analysis. The main drawback of this article is that it focuses on the legal citations of a bill and does not track key elements of lobbying and consulting, such as co-sponsorships, monetary congestion, or other variables. More thought will be needed as to how this can be practically applied to the intended product. However, the article goes into depth on the Louvian method, which can be used by communities and coalitions. Additional research into different forms of centrality is needed.
